results.summary_before: This design generates two independent square waves using 8-bit reloadable countdown timers, with periods proportional to the input values plus one. It also provides a 2-bit sum output of the two square waves. The design is tested by applying arbitrary 8-bit values to the inputs and probing the outputs with an oscilloscope or logic analyzer. External hardware is not required, but the intended use is to drive speakers via resistor dividers and an amplifier.

results.summary_before: This Verilog design generates VGA timing and RGB222 color output for a Tiny VGA PMOD, displaying a bouncing ball animation over an adaptation of Matt Venn's VGA clock. It supports a 640x480 60Hz mode from a 25MHz clock and includes inputs to adjust hours, minutes, and seconds. Testing requires a VGA monitor and Tiny VGA PMOD, with mode and pmod_select inputs configuring the display. The design is notable for combining a real-time clock display with a simple animation and is intended for the IHP tapeout.

results.summary_before: This is a hardware implementation of two-player ping pong rendered on a 16x24 LED matrix, using up/down counters for each paddle and the ball plus an input register to debounce buttons. It requires substantial external hardware: a 16-bit serial-in parallel-out shift register, a 5-to-24 decoder, the LED matrix, eight buttons, BCD counters with 7-segment displays for scoring, and a timing unit to generate the enable and clock signals. Testing can start simply by hooking up left/right buttons for player one and monitoring the horizontal position bits, but full functionality needs the complete external support circuitry. The design is notable for its detailed pin-level documentation and its reliance on external multiplexing and decoding to drive the matrix.

results.summary_before: This is a Verilog replica of the AY-3-8913 programmable sound generator, providing three square-wave tone channels, a white noise generator, and an envelope generator with ten shapes. It is programmed through a multiplexed data/address bus with bus control pins, and it outputs digital 8-bit audio as well as PWM signals for each channel and a master audio output. External hardware such as a DAC, RC filter, amplifier, and speaker are needed to hear the audio, and the design includes a configurable clock divider to match different clock frequencies. The project is notable for its thorough test suite and goal of hardware preservation, fitting on a single Tiny Tapeout tile.

results.summary_before: This is a 12-bit differential (11-bit single-ended) successive-approximation-register ADC implemented with custom metal-fringe capacitors and a calibrated comparator. It samples the input for two clock cycles, performs a binary search conversion over 16 cycles, and outputs the result in two 6-bit halves on the DATA pins synchronized to CLK_DATA. The design supports both differential and single-ended modes, with an offset calibration feature enabled by EN_CAL_OFFSET. Silicon tests show it works at 10-20 MHz but with noticeable noise and missing codes, requiring averaging for accurate results.
